extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, statisticians, and students learning principles of probability and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using probability to judge whether observed concomitances are due to chance or to causal law, and for extending empirical/derived laws to adjacent cases. Emphasizes the role of antecedent frequencies, causal knowledge, repetition, and limits of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use averaging to detect constant causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Small systematic effects (a 'constant cause') can be discovered by comparing average values across conditions or times; e.g., the diurnal variation of the barometer was found by comparing average heights at different hours of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare averages across many instances (hours, trials) to reveal persistent small differences that are constant in the mean even when absolute quantities vary. Example: averaging barometer readings by hour revealed the effect of air rarefaction due to temperature. Anti-pattern: relying on single observations or neglecting averaging that would expose small systematic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for base rates when inferring association
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that two phenomena are connected is measured by the excess of their joint occurrences above the number expected from the antecedent frequency of one of them; if A occurs very commonly, co-occurrence with B may not imply connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always compare observed co-occurrence to the expected co-occurrence given the base-rate (frequency) of each phenomenon. Example: if A exists always, its co-occurrence with B is not evidence of connection. Anti-pattern: counting joint instances alone without reference to how common A or B are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider sampling variability and extreme deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond average expected coincidences, one must consider the likely extent of deviation from that average in smaller samples; the doctrine of chances (theory of probabilities) addresses how often extreme deviations occur by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sample sizes are small, compute or estimate the distribution of possible deviations from the mean to judge whether observed departures are credible by chance. Use probability theory to assess whether an observed deviation is unusually large given sample size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's equally-possible-cases principle
rubrics_metrics.description: "The theory of chances consists in reducing all events of the same kind to a certain number of cases equally possible... The ratio of that number to the number of all the possible cases is the measure of the probability."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this principle when you can legitimately reduce alternatives to mutually exclusive, equally undecided cases (symmetry or verified frequency). Limitation: it requires justification (symmetry or supporting experience) for treating cases as equally possible; otherwise it can mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability is a degree of expectation conditional on evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability is not a quality of an event but 'a mere name for the degree of ground which we... have for expecting it;' it varies with the observer's information (e.g., learning someone has consumption changes the probability they will die this year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always interpret probabilities as conditional on the current state of knowledge. Update probabilities when new evidence arrives. Anti-pattern: treating probability as an intrinsic property of an event independent of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of indifference has limited but valid application
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with no knowledge except a finite set of mutually exclusive possibilities, one may reasonably assign probabilities by symmetry (e.g., equally indifferent among colors) and make decisions accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indifference only when genuinely lacking distinguishing information; be aware that slight, plausible asymmetries in prior knowledge can invalidate equal assignment. Prefer gathering specific information when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer improved data over more elaborate probability calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A very slight improvement in empirical data or taking into fuller account special circumstances is more useful than elaborate application of probabilistic calculus to inferior data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest effort in better observations and in incorporating relevant causal/contextual factors before applying complex formulae. Example: in assessing witness credibility, look at consistency and conduct rather than applying crude lifetime true/false ratios. Anti-pattern: blind use of formulas on poor or inapplicable data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize population averages to heterogeneous individual cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Population averages protect against errors over many cases but are of small value for expecting outcomes in an individual case that may differ greatly from the average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess individual instances using case-specific evidence (consistency, cross-examination, interests, capacities) rather than relying solely on aggregate veracity rates. Use averages only when individual cases don't differ much from the population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware correlated errors when aggregating judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing the number of judges does not guarantee correctness because common prejudices, shared sources of error, or moral effects of large panels can make a wrong decision more likely as numbers increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aggregating opinions, consider dependence/correlation of errors, shared biases, and how institutional changes (e.g., dilution of responsibility) affect judgments. Anti-pattern: assuming independence and applying simple majority-counting arguments without assessing correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground probability estimates in knowledge of comparative frequencies or causes
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate chances, one must possess knowledge of the comparative frequency with which different events or causes occur; probabilities should be based either on specific experiment or deduced from knowledge of the causes' frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, use observed frequencies or reasoned estimates of the frequencies of causes. If causes and their frequencies are accessible, probability estimates based on them are superior to raw empirical frequencies of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal explanations to mere empirical frequency for evaluating probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilities deduced from knowledge of the causes (how often causes favorable vs unfavorable occur) form a higher-order and more secure basis than probabilities drawn simply from past frequencies of the effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, identify and assess the causes and their relative prevalence instead of relying solely on per-enumerationem (simple counting) of past events. Example: actuary's inferences are legitimate because they reflect proportions of causes that prolong life rather than mere past counts of survivors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid induction is required for probability calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability calculations grounded on observed frequencies are themselves inductions; to be legitimate they must be based on valid inductions (i.e., sound generalizations from instances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the induction (sample representativeness, stability of conditions) justifying frequency-to-probability is valid. If induction is invalid, probability figures are unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's Sixth Principle (probability of causes proportional to prior × likelihood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an effect and several possible causes, 'the probability that the effect was produced by any one of these causes is as the antecedent probability of the cause, multiplied by the probability that the cause, if it existed, would have produced the given effect.' (Cases I–III illustrate how priors and likelihoods combine.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this rule to apportion probability among competing causal hypotheses: compute (or reason about) prior plausibility (antecedent probability) and the chance each cause would produce the observed effect if present (likelihood). Examples: Cases I–III show the combinatorial reasoning; apply multiplication of ratios accordingly. This is essentially a Bayesian update principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare antecedent probabilities of chance-combination vs law when assessing coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether a series of coincidences arises from chance or from law, compare the antecedent probability of the chance-combination with that of the law (unknown law's antecedent probability often inestimable); where the chance probability is extremely small, the hypothesis of systematic cause may be preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If antecedent probability of the accidental combination becomes vanishingly small with repetition, and if a plausible non-accidental cause (even of small antecedent probability) could account for it, favor the non-chance explanation. But if the alternative is an unknown law with unquantifiable prior, be cautious—use practical thresholds (extreme excess over expected chance) to accept empirical law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition to distinguish chance from systematic cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of a casual coincidence repeating n times falls rapidly (product of single-event probabilities); therefore repeated occurrence of a specific coincidence quickly makes accidental origin unlikely compared to a systematic cause (e.g., repeated aces suggesting loaded die).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat experiments when possible to see whether improbably repeated outcomes persist; calculate how the probability of pure chance decreases with independent repetitions (e.g., 1/6^n for n aces). When repetition yields events far rarer than expected by chance, infer systematic cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undiscovered laws are hard to quantify; accept empirical law when excess coincidences are extremely unlikely by chance
rubrics_metrics.description: When the antecedent probability of an unknown law cannot be estimated, practical decisions rest on whether the observed excess of coincidences over chance would itself be an exceedingly uncommon event; if so, the coincidence may be received as an empirical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits: you generally cannot numerically compare priors of unknown laws to chance. Use heuristics: if observed excess is so extreme under chance that its occurrence would be very improbable, adopt the causal hypothesis subject to future correction by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative laws have inferior generality and certainty to ultimate laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative or secondary uniformities (co-existence/sequence of effects) are less general and more contingent than ultimate causal laws because they often depend on specific collocations of several primeval causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat derivative laws as conditionally valid: they hold where the necessary collocation of causes is known to obtain. Do not assume derivative uniformities apply outside observed contexts without examining underlying cause collocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit extension of derivative laws to known collocations/conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities (e.g., conjunctions of effects) are admissible only within the conditions of time and place confirmed by actual observation, because changes in collocations or supervening counteracting causes can invalidate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extrapolating derivative laws to adjacent cases or the future, check that the collocations of primeval causes remain the same. Example: the alternation of day and night depends on Earth's rotation and single sun; adding a second sun or stopping rotation would invalidate the derivative uniformity even if the underlying causal laws remain true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for counteracting causes when assessing derived uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an underlying cause remains operative, a supervening cause that counteracts one of the contributing causes can destroy the derivative uniformity (e.g., day need not be followed by night if produced by different causes on another body).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate potential external or counteracting influences before extending an observed uniformity. Anti-pattern: assuming that because an ultimate law holds, all derivative patterns based on it must hold universally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use causal knowledge to justify extrapolation to future or adjacent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary confident inferences about the future (e.g., that the sun will rise tomorrow) rely on knowledge of the causes producing the derivative uniformity, not merely on the past sequence of observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extrapolating beyond observed instances, make explicit the causal mechanisms that support the extrapolation and assess their stability across the extrapolated domain. Extrapolation lacking causal justification is fragile.
